figures.caption: Figure 1. Machine learning interatomic potential training workflow. Workflow begins by sampling representative interfacial, dis- ordered, glassy amorphous, and crystalline structures from AIMD. Active learning loop begins with r2SCAN database generation extracted from sampled structure, model training, and validation of prediction accuracy, stability performance, and dynamic properties.

Figure 2. Spatiotemporal evolution of local bonding environments at the Na3PS4/Na interface from the NpT ML-MD simula- tion, capturing the coordination numbers of (a) P–P, (b) Na–S, (c) Na–P, and (d) P–Na. Each pair denotes a central atom (first element) coordinated with neighboring atoms (second element). Each pixel represents the mean coordination number averaged over all central atoms of the given species within that time and relative-z bin. As a result, values below unity do not indicate frac- tional bonds on individual atoms but rather that only a fraction of the central atoms in that region have a neighbor of the paired species. Blue dashed lines indicate interphase boundaries from the Li7P3S11/Li system [19] for growth rate comparison.

Figure 3. Structural comparison of sulfide-rich layer regions in the (a) Na3PS4/Na and (b) Li7P3S11/Li. The red circles show the identified nanocrystalline domains which exhibits crystal symmetry of the Na2S or Li2S structures. Reprinted with permission from [19]. Copyright (2025) American Chemical Society.

Figure 4. Ionic flux of P calculated from the Onsager transport coefficients for (a) Na–P–S and (b) Li-P-S. Positive flux is in the direction of the metal anode, whereas negative flux is directed towards the solid state electrolyte. (c), (d) maps the magnitude of the Onsager transport coefficients responsible for calculating the ionic fluxes, for Na and Li respectively. (b) and (d) Reprinted with permission from [19]. Copyright (2025) American Chemical Society.

Figure 5. Na–P connectivity pathway analysis of the Na3PS4/Na interphase at 10 ns. (a) Three-dimensional visualization of the Na–P network within the interphase region, whereby highlighted regions demonstrates clusters that span from the SSE layer to the metal anode layer. Red points indicate P atoms belonging to the connective cluster; blue points indicate Na atoms in the cluster; gray points indicate atoms not connected to the cluster. (b) X–Z projection showing lateral extent of the percolating network. (c) Z-distribution of atoms showing percolation spanning from the Na3PS4 solid electrolyte to the Na metal anode. The connected cluster forms immediately upon interface contact and persists throughout the 10 ns simulation.

Figure 6. Schematic of the layered interphase structure at the Na3PS4/Na interface after 10 ns of ML-MD simulation. Three com- positionally distinct regions are identified: a Na–S-rich layer adjacent to the Na metal anode, a mixed Na–S–P interphase layer, and a Na–P-rich layer extending toward the Na3PS4 solid electrolyte. A continuous Na–P bond connectivity network (high- lighted) spans the full interphase thickness from the Na metal to the Na3PS4 side, providing a topological basis for electronic percolation through the semiconducting Na–P phases.

figures.label: S12
figures.caption: Figure S12: Na–S partial radial distribution function of the interphase Na2S-rich region (blue, aver- aged over the ﬁnal ﬁve frames at 10.5 ns) compared with crystalline antiﬂuorite Na2S (red). Both share a sharp ﬁrst coordination shell at ∼2.8 ˚A (intact Na–S bonding), but the interphase RDF decays to g(r) ≈1 beyond the ﬁrst shell, whereas the crystalline reference retains sharp peaks throughout the long-range-order region (r > 4 ˚A, shaded). The translational-order parameter τ and the relative second/third-shell peak heights (inset) are suppressed ∼5-fold in the interphase, quantifying its amorphous character.

figures.label: S13
figures.caption: Figure S13: Percolation probability as a function of bond cutoﬀdistance, computed over frames sampled across the 10 ns trajectory. (left) P–P-only network as a function of the P–P cutoﬀ: no percolation occurs at any cutoﬀ. (center) Mixed Na–P network as the P–P cutoﬀis varied with the Na–P cutoﬀﬁxed at 3.2 ˚A: percolation is constant (∼90%) and independent of the P–P cutoﬀ. (right) Mixed Na–P network as the Na–P cutoﬀis varied with the P–P cutoﬀﬁxed at 2.5 ˚A: percolation plateaus for cutoﬀs ≥3.1 ˚A and collapses only below the Na–P bond distance (∼3.0 ˚A). Dashed lines indicate the cutoﬀvalues used in this work.

figures.label: S14
figures.caption: Figure S14: Temporal evolution of interphase connectivity over the 10 ns trajectory (P–P cutoﬀ2.5 ˚A, Na–P cutoﬀ3.2 ˚A). (top) Percolation status per frame: the mixed Na–P network ﬁrst percolates at 0.23 ns and remains percolating in 99.8% of subsequent frames (1035/1060 frames overall, 97.6%), whereas the P–P-only network never percolates. (second) Fractional z-span of the largest connected cluster, which grows to approach the full interphase thickness. (third) Size of the largest connected component, reaching ∼5000 atoms for the Na–P network versus ∼10 for P–P. (bottom) Total number of bond edges in each network, increasing monotonically as the interphase grows.
